title: API 653 Training in Chicago: Tank Inspector Exam Prep
description: API 653 exam prep for Chicago tank inspectors: Argo, Lake Calumet, Griffith and refinery tank farms, ethanol and caustic service, self-paced online.
h1: API 653 training in Chicago: exam preparation for aboveground storage tank inspectors at terminals, refineries and pipeline tank farms
html:
API 653 exam prep for tank inspectors in the Chicago region

Chicago holds a great deal of aboveground storage. Crude arrives by pipeline from the north and west and waits in tank farms in north-west Indiana; refined products, ethanol and chemicals move through terminals along the Sanitary and Ship Canal, the Calumet River and Lake Calumet; and three refineries keep their own tank fields of crude, intermediates, products and asphalt. Most of the field-erected tanks among them are inspected periodically to API 653, and its formal inspections need an inspector who holds the API 653 Aboveground Storage Tank Inspector certification.

Atlantis NDT's API 653 course prepares you for that examination. It is a self-paced online course with instructor Q&A: you begin when you enrol, study around the terminal or refinery schedule, and put questions to the instructor whenever a clause or calculation will not come out. There is no Atlantis classroom in Chicago. The American Petroleum Institute decides who is eligible, administers the exam in person at Prometric test centres and issues the certification.

Chicagoland tank farms, in the operators' own figures

The table lists published figures from the operators themselves. It is not a complete list of the region's storage, but it shows the range of tanks an API 653 inspector meets here.

Operator and siteWhat the operator publishesServices stored
Kinder Morgan, Argo terminal on the Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal218 tanks from 50,000 gallons to 95,000 barrels, about 2.67 million barrels in all, on 145 acres with three barge docksPetroleum, chemicals, ethanol, biodiesel and residual fuel oil, with product heating offered
Kinder Morgan, Chicago terminal on the Calumet River and Lake Calumet86 tanks from 12,000 gallons to 55,000 barrels, about 789,000 barrels, on 178 acres with ship and barge docksChemicals, ethanol, biodiesel, caustics, acids, deicer products and vegetable oils
Enbridge, Griffith and Hartsdale terminals in IndianaShell capacity of 2.8 million barrels at Griffith and about 1.5 million at Hartsdale, near ScherervilleCrude oil moving between the Lakehead system and refineries in the Midwest and beyond
Buckeye, Chicago ComplexEast Chicago, Hammond, Hartsdale and Peotone facilities, marketed as one complex since 2011 and put at about 6.8 million barrels of storage when Buckeye announced an expansion in 2018Petroleum products, with product blending tankage added in that expansion
ExxonMobil, Joliet areaTankage and LPG storage at the refinery, plus terminals or tank farms at Des Plaines, Lockport, Hammond and MokenaRefinery feed and products; LPG in pressure storage, which is outside API 653
bp, Whiting refinery435,000 barrels per calendar day of crude distillation in EIA's 2026 listing; the Indiana Department of Environmental Management credits it with 7% of all asphalt produced in the United StatesCrude, intermediates, products and heated asphalt

Two practical points follow. The size range is wide, from 12,000-gallon tanks to field-erected tanks of 95,000 barrels and more, so an inspector needs to know which standard applies to which. And the services vary more than on a typical crude terminal: ethanol, caustic, acid, heated asphalt and vegetable oil all bring their own damage and their own inspection priorities.

Which rules bring an API 653 inspector to a Chicago tank

EPA's SPCC rule

Non-transportation facilities above the federal 1,320-gallon threshold for aboveground oil storage need a Spill Prevention, Control and Countermeasure plan, and 40 CFR 112.8(c)(6) requires integrity testing of their aboveground bulk storage containers on a regular schedule and after material repairs. EPA's own fact sheet names API 653 as the standard typically used for field-erected tanks and STI SP001 for shop-fabricated and small field-erected tanks. It says the formal in-service external and out-of-service internal inspections under API 653 must be done by an API 653 certified inspector, while frequent external visual checks can often be made by trained facility staff. Records must be kept for three years, and EPA recommends keeping formal test records for the life of the container.

Pipeline breakout tanks

Tanks that serve a hazardous liquid pipeline as breakout tanks, as many at Griffith and Hartsdale do, come under 49 CFR 195.432. Atmospheric and low-pressure steel breakout tanks must be inspected to API Std 653, but without its risk-based alternative for internal intervals. Breakout tanks built to API Std 2510, such as pressurised LPG storage, are inspected under section 6 of API 510 instead, which is a reminder that a sphere or bullet is not an API 653 tank at all.

State fire codes

Illinois's Office of the State Fire Marshal writes rules for aboveground bulk storage tanks at bulk plants and terminals (41 Ill. Adm. Code 160) and for fuel dispensing tanks (Part 180) under the Gasoline Storage Act. In Indiana, the Department of Environmental Management notes that the Department of Homeland Security runs a plan review for tanks storing flammable and combustible liquids, under the State Fire Marshal's rules. These rules sit beside API 653 rather than replacing it, and none of them is examined.

Ethanol, caustic, acid and asphalt: what Chicago products do to tanks

The API 653 Body of Knowledge for the current windows selects ten mechanisms from API RP 571, and Chicago terminals give a working example of nearly every one of them:

  • Ethanol stress corrosion cracking (3.28) in carbon steel tanks storing fuel-grade ethanol, which both Kinder Morgan terminals handle. Cracking tends to appear at welds and other highly stressed areas, so crack detection methods, not thickness gauging, find it.
  • Caustic corrosion and caustic stress corrosion cracking (3.14 and 3.15) in caustic soda storage, where temperature, concentration and whether welds were stress relieved decide the risk.
  • Sulfuric acid corrosion (3.62) in acid storage, where velocity at nozzles and the acid strength matter more than average shell loss.
  • Corrosion under insulation (3.22) on heated, insulated tanks such as asphalt and residual fuel oil storage, whose shells may run in or cycle through the CUI temperature range.
  • Soil corrosion (3.57) on the underside of bottoms, the reason floors are scanned and API RP 651 cathodic protection is in the Body of Knowledge, and microbiologically influenced corrosion (3.45), which can attack under water bottoms on the product side as well; RP 652 covers the internal bottom linings that protect that side.
  • Atmospheric and concentration cell corrosion (3.8 and 3.19) at shell-to-bottom joints, under deposits and at crevices where water stands.
  • Brittle fracture (3.11), the mechanism a Chicago winter keeps on the list.

Heated tanks bring one further exam point. The Body of Knowledge includes the thickness required for hydrotesting and for elevated temperatures, so a heated asphalt tank's shell evaluation is not simply a copy of the ambient-temperature case.

Cold weather: design metal temperature and impact testing

Brittle fracture is a real concern for older tanks in a northern climate, and the exam tests the reasoning around it. API 653 asks the inspector to evaluate the risk of failure by brittle fracture, and the impact testing calculations in the Body of Knowledge draw on API 650. The starting point is the design metal temperature: the lowest one-day mean ambient temperature for the location, read from the isotherm map in API 650, plus 15°F. If a problem places a tank where the map reads −10°F, the design metal temperature is 5°F.

With that figure, the material group from API 650's tables and the governing plate thickness, you read the impact test exemption curves to decide whether a replacement or insert plate needs Charpy testing. Where the plate's material group, thickness and design metal temperature fall on the wrong side of the curve, the plate must be impact tested, and the figure's notes decide the edge cases, so read them rather than a remembered rule of thumb. The exam typically gives you the temperatures and expects you to carry them through the figure correctly, so practise that lookup in the PDF until it is routine. For an inspector at a Griffith crude tank or a lakeside terminal, the same reasoning decides whether an old shell's history is good enough to keep it in cold service.

Worked example: settlement survey points on a large crude tank

The Body of Knowledge lists the number of settlement survey points as a calculation in its own right, alongside edge settlement, bottom settlement near the shell and localized settlement away from it. API 653 Annex B sets the rule for shell survey points: at least eight, spaced no more than 32 ft apart around the circumference.

  1. Take a 200 ft diameter crude tank of the size found in pipeline tank farms. Circumference = π × 200 = 628.3 ft.
  2. Points needed at 32 ft maximum spacing = 628.3 ÷ 32 = 19.6, rounded up to 20.
  3. Twenty is more than the minimum of eight, so 20 points govern. For a 60 ft diameter products tank the circumference is 188.5 ft, the spacing rule gives 5.9, rounded up to 6, and the minimum of eight governs instead.

Once the elevations are surveyed, the evaluation separates uniform settlement and rigid-body tilt from the out-of-plane component that actually stresses the shell. Ground that freezes and thaws under a tank pad gives Chicago inspectors plenty of settlement data to interpret, and the tank settlement measurement guide covers the acceptance side in more depth.

Routes into API 653 for Chicago tank people

API 653 eligibility follows Annex D of the standard: education plus storage tank experience gained in the last ten years while employed by, or under contract with, an authorized inspection agency. The API 653 certification requirements page has the detail. Locally, candidates come from four directions:

  • NDT technicians who scan floors with magnetic flux leakage, gauge shells and inspect welds at terminals and refinery tank fields;
  • tank construction and repair crews, whose fabrication and repair years count towards the longer routes as long as at least one year is spent supervising or performing inspection;
  • terminal operators and maintenance staff, whose operating experience with tanks counts in the same way, and who often move into the terminal's inspection role;
  • engineers with a bachelor's degree in engineering or technology, who need one year of supervising or performing tank inspection.

Studying API 653 around the Chicago tank season

Out-of-service tank work around Chicago often bunches into the warmer months, when many owners prefer to clean, open, repair and hydrotest, so a tank inspector's quiet season is often the winter. That makes the colder months the natural time for the heavy reading, and spring and autumn the time to aim an exam window at, depending on your own site's programme.

Most of the open-book difficulty sits in API 650 rather than API 653. The current Body of Knowledge excludes most API 650 annexes and all but specified paragraphs of a few others, and it limits welding procedure review to SMAW or GMAW on P-No. 1 base metals. Learn where API 650 puts the shell, bottom, roof and testing rules, because the open-book questions send you there. Build the calculations, from the locally thinned area and pitting checks to bottom plate minimum remaining thickness and lap-welded patch plates, until you can do them without hesitation, and send the instructor the ones that will not reconcile. Free API 653 practice questions are a quick way to find the gaps.

The examination is sat in person at a Prometric test centre, and Prometric lists centres in and around Chicago. API runs it in set windows with application deadlines; the exam schedule page linked below keeps the current ones.

Sponsoring tank inspectors from a Chicago terminal or refinery

Terminal operators and refinery tank teams often want more than one certified inspector, both to cover SPCC and breakout tank programmes and to have someone on hand when a tank comes out of service. A single enquiry can include the whole tank team, with fees quoted on request. Each person studies at their own pace, applies to API individually and sits the examination individually. In the United States Atlantis performs UT, MT, PT and VT inspection but no radiography, and its tank inspection services for Chicago describe the field side; the API 653 tank inspection guide gives a wider view of the code.

faq.q: Is there an API 653 class I can attend in Chicago?
faq.a: Not from Atlantis. There is no Atlantis classroom in the Chicago area; the API 653 course is online and self-paced, with an instructor answering your questions, and you can start as soon as you enrol. Some other providers run seminars on fixed dates. Whatever preparation you choose, the examination itself is taken in person at a Prometric test centre once API has accepted your application.

faq.q: Who may do the monthly walk-round at an Argo-area terminal, and who must do the formal internal inspection?
faq.a: EPA's SPCC guidance says frequent external visual inspections can often be made by trained facility personnel, while the formal in-service external and out-of-service internal inspections under API 653 must be carried out by an API 653 certified inspector. The facility's SPCC plan, prepared under the rule and certified where required, records which standard it follows and the schedule.

faq.q: Our terminal stores ethanol and caustic soda. Which damage mechanisms should I study first?
faq.a: Ethanol stress corrosion cracking, caustic corrosion and caustic stress corrosion cracking are all among the ten RP 571 mechanisms in the current API 653 Body of Knowledge. Learn the conditions that make tanks susceptible, where the damage appears and which inspection methods find it. Add soil corrosion and MIC for the floors and brittle fracture for cold service, because those are examined too.

faq.q: Do breakout tanks at Griffith follow different inspection rules from refinery tanks?
faq.a: Yes. Breakout tanks fall under 49 CFR 195.432, which requires inspection to API 653 but excludes its risk-based procedure for setting internal intervals, and sends breakout tanks built to API 2510 to API 510 instead. Refinery and terminal tanks outside a pipeline system follow API 653 and the owner's programme, subject to SPCC and state rules. A 2026 PHMSA proposal would change the breakout tank position, so check the current text.

faq.q: I run MFL floor scans in north-west Indiana. Does that count toward API 653?
faq.a: It can. Floor scanning, shell gauging and weld examination done as part of a tank inspection programme are inspection activities, provided the work was done while employed by or under contract to an authorized inspection agency. With a high school diploma API asks for three years of tank experience, including a year of performing or supervising inspection. Record the tanks and tasks as you go.

faq.q: Do I need to know Illinois or Indiana tank rules for the API 653 exam?
faq.a: No. The exam is national and draws only on the publications listed in the Body of Knowledge and the Publications Effectivity Sheet for your window: API 653 and API 650, the recommended practices and the ASME sections named there. State fire code and environmental rules matter on the job in Chicago, but none of them is examined.

faq.q: How should I handle API 650 in the open-book half?
faq.a: Treat it as a map rather than a book to read cover to cover. The Body of Knowledge excludes most of its annexes, so learn where the material, shell design, bottom, roof, welding and testing sections are, and practise finding the impact test figures and tables quickly in a plain PDF. Many open-book questions are lost to searching, not to not knowing.

faq.q: Can our Chicago terminal put its whole tank team through API 653 prep together?
faq.a: Yes. One enquiry listing the candidates and the exam windows they are aiming at gets a quote for the group. Each person works through the course at their own pace with access to the instructor, then applies to API and sits the exam individually. Check each candidate's documented tank experience against Annex D before enrolling them, because API decides eligibility case by case.
